title: Bull Flag
teaches: The bull flag as we trade it: a leader above the 200-day and a rising 50-day makes a fast pole, rests a few sessions in a quiet drift that holds the 21-day EMA, and is bought at market when a trigger level trades, with the stop a few cents under the day's low, a third off at 3R and 5R, the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop as the planned cost.

facts.quote: A flag is a small rectangle pattern that slopes against the previous trend.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag is a small rectangle sloping against the prior trend.

facts.quote: Flags and pennants require evidence of a sharp advance or decline in heavy volume.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag needs a sharp advance on heavy volume before it.

facts.quote: The flagpole is the distance from the first resistance or support break to the high or low of the flag/pennant.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: the flagpole runs from the first break to the flag's high.

facts.quote: Ideally, these patterns will form between one and four weeks.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: ideally a flag forms in one to four weeks.

facts.quote: An expansion of volume on the resistance (support) break lends credence to the validity of the formation
facts.claim: ChartSchool: rising volume on the break adds credence.

facts.quote: Once a flag is over 12 weeks old, it would be classified as a rectangle.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a flag older than 12 weeks is a rectangle.

facts.quote: The flagpole which leads to the flag should be unusually steep and last several days.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the flagpole should be unusually steep and last several days.

facts.quote: If you don't have a straight-line (or a quick move) price run (the flagpole), then you don't have a flag.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: no straight-line run, no flag.

facts.quote: Looks like a small rectangle often tilted against the prevailing price trend.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a flag looks like a small rectangle tilted against the trend.

facts.quote: Flags are short, less than 3 weeks long. Patterns longer than that are rectangles or channels.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: flags are under 3 weeks; longer patterns are rectangles or channels.

facts.quote: Downward trend 74% (up breakouts) to 77% (down breakouts) of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: volume trends down inside a flag 74% of the time for up breakouts.

facts.quote: The best performance comes when the inbound trend is upward leading to a flag which tilts downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the best flags tilt down after an upward trend.

facts.quote: A tight flag performs better than a loose one.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a tight flag performs better than a loose one.

facts.quote: A loose flag is one in which price meanders, pokes outside the trendline boundary, contains white space, or looks jagged.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a loose flag meanders, pokes outside its lines and looks jagged.

facts.quote: Look for a near vertical price run, preferably lasting several days.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's earnings flag: a near vertical run lasting several days.

facts.quote: Near the top of the flagpole, price consolidates and usually trends downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's earnings flag: the pause near the top usually trends down.

facts.quote: Buy when price pierces a flag or pennant trendline (D in the figure to the right) or rises above the event pattern's high (A), but not before.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: buy the trendline pierce or the move above the pattern's high, not before.

facts.quote: A big move higher sometime in the past 1-3 months. This move can be anywhere from 30-100%+ and usually lasts a few days to a few weeks.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a big move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months comes first.

facts.quote: An orderly pullback and consolidation with higher lows and tightening range in the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: an orderly pullback with higher lows and a tightening range.

facts.quote: During the consolidation the stock price "surfs" the rising 10- and 20-day. and sometimes toe 50-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: in the consolidation price surfs the rising 10- and 20-day, sometimes toes the 50-day.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: I don't find it as effective and more skill and experience is needed.
facts.claim: Kullamagi finds anticipating the breakout less effective.

facts.quote: You should sell 1/3 to 1/2 of the position after 3-5 days, and then move the stop to break even.
facts.claim: Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, then moves the stop to breakeven.

facts.quote: The rest of the position should be trailed with the 10- or the 20-day moving average.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails the rest with the 10- or 20-day average.

facts.quote: they tend to move in stair steps. Meaning they will make a 20-50%+ move, pull back and go sideways for a while, then make another move.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: leaders move in stair steps: a move, a sideways rest, another move.

facts.quote: day before breakout should be narrow range day or negative day
facts.claim: Bonde: the day before the breakout should be a narrow-range or down day.

facts.quote: volume on breakout day should be higher
facts.claim: Bonde: breakout-day volume should be higher.

facts.quote: stock should close near high on breakout day
facts.claim: Bonde: the breakout day should close near its high.

facts.quote: High tight flags and bull flags are the most common continuation patterns on highly ranked stock by 65 day momentum.
facts.claim: Bonde: flags are the most common continuation patterns on momentum leaders.

facts.quote: Many of these powerful momentum movers have very shallow corrections before they continue onward.
facts.claim: Bonde: momentum movers often correct very shallowly before continuing.

facts.quote: Many times the stock will form bull flag so late in the move that you would miss bulk of the possible returns by waiting for the bull flag.
facts.claim: Bonde: a flag can form so late in a move that waiting for it misses most of the return.

facts.quote: They are typically seen right after a big, quick move.
facts.claim: Zanger: flags come right after a big, quick move.

facts.quote: Bullish flags are characterized by lower tops and lower bottoms, with the pattern slanting against the trend. But unlike wedges, their trend lines run parallel.
facts.claim: Zanger: a bull flag has lower tops and bottoms, slanting against the trend, with parallel lines.

facts.quote: Volume generally contracts during the pause with an increase on the breakout.
facts.claim: Zanger: volume contracts in the pause and rises on the breakout.

facts.quote: A minor reversal down in a bull trend. Traders expect the bull trend to resume.
facts.claim: Brooks: his bull flag is any minor reversal down in a bull trend.

facts.quote: It can be as brief as one sideways bar or it can retrace most of the most recent leg up.
facts.claim: Brooks: his bull flag can be one bar or retrace most of the last leg.

facts.quote: Most truly sound patterns consolidate a minimum of seven to eight weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: most sound bases consolidate at least seven to eight weeks; it lists no ordinary flag.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average.
facts.claim: C29: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part into a climax run on your own long.

facts.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
facts.claim: D39: entry, stop and size written down before the open.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: E52: trail the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: D38: A and B normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.

facts.quote: The close is above the 200-day simple moving average on every flag session and at the entry.
facts.claim: The close is above the 200-day on every flag session and at the entry.

facts.quote: The 50-day SMA is above the 200-day SMA and higher than it was 10 sessions ago, and the close is above the 50-day.
facts.claim: The 50-day is above the 200-day and rising, with the close above the 50-day.

facts.quote: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is the A+ case; the second is normal; the third or later flag in one run without a proper base is graded B- or passed.
facts.claim: The first flag after a breakout or a correction is A+; the third or later without a base is B- or a pass.

facts.quote: A flag that forms right after a parabolic burst is treated as extended until the 10-day average catches up: no entry while the flag's closes sit more than 10% above the 10-day SMA.
facts.claim: A flag right after a parabolic burst is extended until the 10-day catches up.

facts.quote: A flag that makes a higher high than the pole is no longer a flag; it has broken out (the T3 trigger).
facts.claim: A flag that makes a higher high than the pole has broken out.

facts.quote: A flag of 16 to 20 sessions is B- at best. Past 20 sessions it is a base, judged as a flat base or a VCP.
facts.claim: A flag of 16 to 20 sessions is B- at best; past 20 it is a base.

facts.quote: The flag drifts sideways or down: the least-squares slope of the flag's highs is at or below zero. Higher highs and higher lows through the pause is a wedge up, not a flag.
facts.claim: The flag drifts sideways or down; higher highs and higher lows is a wedge up, not a flag.

facts.quote: The flag's average daily range (high minus low, as a percent of the close) is smaller than the pole's.
facts.claim: The flag's average daily range is smaller than the pole's.

facts.quote: No flag session closes red with volume of 1.5 times its 50-day average or more. One such day drops the grade; two end the flag.
facts.claim: One heavy red day in the flag drops the grade; two end the flag.

facts.quote: Every flag session closes at or above the rising 21-day EMA. An intraday undercut that closes back above is allowed and is often the buy.
facts.claim: Every flag close holds the rising 21-day EMA; an intraday undercut that closes back above is allowed.

facts.quote: Riding the 9-day or 10-day average through the flag is the A+ version; tagging the 20-day or 21-day EMA and reclaiming it is the A or B version.
facts.claim: Riding the 9 or 10-day through the flag is A+; tagging the 20 or 21-day and reclaiming is A or B.

facts.quote: An inside day or a narrow-range day right before the trigger is the A+ tightness cue: it gives a nearer stop.
facts.claim: An inside day or narrow-range day right before the trigger is the A+ tightness cue.

facts.quote: A market order when the trigger level trades, regular hours only. Set the alert at the level the night before.
facts.claim: A market order when the trigger level trades, regular hours only; alert set the night before.

facts.quote: The flag's low is the idea's invalidation, not the default stop. It is almost never a 3% stop.
facts.claim: The flag's low is the invalidation, not the default stop.

facts.quote: Before entry: two or more heavy red days in the flag, each on 1.5 times average volume or more. Distribution, not a rest.
facts.claim: Two or more heavy red days in the flag is distribution, not a rest.

facts.quote: Before entry: the pause slopes up (higher highs and higher lows). A wedge up, not a flag.
facts.claim: A pause that slopes up is a wedge up, not a flag.

facts.quote: Before entry: the third flag in a short run without a proper base. Wait for the base.
facts.claim: The third flag in a short run without a base: wait for the base.

facts.quote: After the entry, a close under the flag's low means the idea is dead; the stop has normally been hit well before it.
facts.claim: After entry a close under the flag's low means the idea is dead; the stop is hit well before.

facts.quote: Measure the pole. A bull flag follows a 20% to 30% run in 20 sessions or fewer; a high tight flag follows a near-double, 90% or more in 40 sessions or fewer, and rests 5 to 30 sessions.
facts.claim: The tell against the high tight flag: measure the pole; the HTF follows a near-double.

facts.quote: Count the sessions since the pole top. A flag is done in 3 to 15 sessions and is a base past 20; a flat base rests at least 25 sessions in a box up to 15% deep
facts.claim: The tell against the flat base: count the sessions; a flat base is a long box with a tapped ceiling.

facts.quote: Look for shrinking pullbacks. A flag is one short drift on lighter volume; a VCP strings two to six pullbacks over 15 sessions or more, each smaller than the last, before its pivot.
facts.claim: The tell against the VCP: a flag is one drift; a VCP strings shrinking pullbacks.

facts.quote: Find the pole. A flag needs a 20% run in the 20 sessions before the rest; a pullback to the 10, 20 or 50-day with no pole is a moving-average pullback, setup 12.
facts.claim: The tell against the moving-average pullback: find the pole; no pole, no flag.

facts.quote: Buying the pole or chasing far above the trigger.
facts.claim: A named mistake: buying the pole or chasing far above the trigger.

facts.quote: Calling a deep, loose, jagged pullback a flag. Bulkowski: a loose flag meanders and looks jagged.
facts.claim: A named mistake: calling a deep, loose, jagged pullback a flag.

facts.quote: Using the flag low as the stop when it is 8% to 15% away, then sizing too big or skipping the stop-width check.
facts.claim: A named mistake: the flag low as the stop, then sizing too big.

facts.quote: Sitting in a forever flag with no trigger
facts.claim: A named mistake: sitting in a forever flag with no trigger.

facts.quote: Adding to a flag trade or averaging down.
facts.claim: A named mistake: adding to a flag trade or averaging down.

facts.quote: Expecting the shape alone to pay. Measured, it does not: whatever edge there is comes from the leader, the catalyst, the market and the management.
facts.claim: A named mistake: expecting the shape alone to pay; the edge is the leader, the catalyst, the market and the management.

facts.quote: Reading Brooks's bull flag (any pullback in a bull trend) as this setup. Ours needs a pole.
facts.claim: Brooks's bull flag is any pullback; ours needs a pole.

facts.quote: bf.which_flag: the first flag after a base breakout or a market correction
facts.claim: The A+ row: the first flag after a base breakout or a market correction.

facts.quote: bf.which_flag: the third or later flag
facts.claim: The B- row: the third or later flag.

facts.claim: The B- row: a Yellow market.

facts.quote: bf.market_reading: Red, or Orange unless A+
facts.claim: No trade: Red, or Orange unless A+.

facts.claim: Seven in ten fixed-stop flag entries come back to the stop before 3R; the small stop and the next trigger are the answer.

facts.quote: A pole of 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst, an HVE or an earnings gap, is the A+ pole.
facts.claim: The A+ pole is made fast on a catalyst, such as an earnings gap.

facts.quote: A few cents under the low of the entry day, or under the prior day's low when that is the planned stop.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the entry day's low, or the prior day's low when that is the plan.

facts.quote: Trail the last third: a close under the 10-day for a fast mover, under the 21-day for a steadier one.
facts.claim: Trail the last third on the 10-day or the 21-day.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop. No starter, no adding to a flag trade, no averaging down.
facts.claim: Full size at one price with one stop; no starter, no adds.

facts.quote: No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. A post-earnings flag is fine.
facts.claim: No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report; a post-earnings flag is fine.

facts.quote: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is the best one.
facts.claim: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is the best one.

facts.quote: A real stop order with the broker. It only moves up.
facts.claim: A real stop order with the broker; it only moves up.

facts.quote: Time stop: still under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.
facts.claim: Time stop: under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.

facts.quote: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out if that is past 2R.
facts.claim: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out past 2R.

facts.claim: A named mistake: waiting for a confirmation breakout and getting stopped in the chop below it.

walkthroughs.title: SHOP, May 2020: the flag that held the 21-day
steps: SHOP, spring 2020. The stock doubled in 12 days to 66.57, then rested eight sessions, 59.50 to 66.26.
Every close of the flag held the rising 21-day EMA. Volume ran 0.85x the pole's. Above the 50 and 200-day.
2020-05-04: it trades over the prior day's high. Buy at market, 62.80, under the flag's high. Stop 61.65.
Failure mode: the break stalls and rolls back through the entry day's low. Instead it ran to 41.7R.

walkthroughs.title: AMD, August 2018: four quiet days after an earnings gap
steps: AMD, 2018. An earnings-gap pole: 29% in 14 days to 20.28. Then four days, 18.73 to 20.10, on 0.75x volume.
Our kind of flag: short and shallow, the pole on a catalyst. The pause is 7.6% deep.
2018-08-21: the prior day's high breaks. Buy at market, 20.09. Stop a few cents under the low, 19.81, 1.4% away.
A third at 3R, a third at 5R, the rest on the trail. It ran from 20 to 34 in five weeks.

walkthroughs.title: RARE, May 2015: a staircase, one step at a time
steps: RARE, 2015. A 53% pole in 13 days to 85.93, then four days resting at the 10-day EMA, 80.25 to 85.79.
2015-05-27: it trades over the prior day's high before the flag's high breaks. Buy at market, 83.26.
Stop a few cents under the low, 81.18, 2.5% away. Full size at one price, one stop. No starter, no adds.
Then a second leg the same size. You hold what is left on the trail, with no adds on the way.

questions.q: What has to come right before a bull flag?
choices: A sharp, fast run up in days
A long flat base of many weeks
A quick drop on bad news
A slow, steady grind higher
questions.answer: A sharp, fast run up in days
questions.why: A sharp, fast run up, the pole. Bulkowski: without a straight-line run there is no flag, and the pole should be unusually steep. ChartSchool wants evidence of a sharp advance on heavy volume. Zanger sees flags right after a big, quick move. A slow grind is not a pole.
questions.lesson_line: No pole, no flag. The run is what the rest is resting from.

wrong.A long flat base of many weeks: A base can come before the run, but the flag itself follows the run.
wrong.A quick drop on bad news: A drop is not a pole. The pole is a fast run up, and the flag rests after it.
wrong.A slow, steady grind higher: A slow grind is not a pole. Bulkowski: the flagpole should be unusually steep.

questions.simple: A bull flag comes right after a sharp, fast run up, called the pole. With no pole there is no flag.

deeper.trap: A neat, tight pause is not enough. If the run before it was slow, there is no pole and so no flag. Bulkowski is blunt: no straight-line run, no flag.

reasons: +1 fixed before (the Bulkowski steep-pole quote was added to the cited facts)

questions.q: Which way does a bull flag drift while it rests?
choices: Sideways or down against the trend
Up, with higher highs and lows
Straight down to the 200-day
Flat only; a tilt down is a failure
questions.answer: Sideways or down against the trend
questions.why: Sideways or down, against the trend. ChartSchool: a flag is a small rectangle that slopes against the previous trend. Zanger: lower tops and lower bottoms, with parallel lines. Bulkowski: the best flags tilt down after an upward trend. Rising highs and lows make a wedge up, not a flag.
questions.lesson_line: The flag leans back against the run. Up and to the right is something else.

wrong.Up, with higher highs and lows: Higher highs and higher lows is a wedge up, not a flag.
wrong.Straight down to the 200-day: Our card lets a flag give back at most half the pole and at most 15% from the pole top. A slide to the 200-day is not a rest.
wrong.Flat only; a tilt down is a failure: Bulkowski: the best flags tilt down after an upward trend. Zanger: lower tops and lower bottoms.

questions.simple: A bull flag drifts sideways or down while it rests. It leans against the run and does not climb.

reasons: three agreeing web sources, a stable definition

questions.q: The flag stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low, or the prior day's low if that is the plan.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low, or under the prior day's low when that is the plan. Stop first, then size from it. Kullamagi also uses the low of the day, and no wider than the stock's usual daily range.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first. The day's low, a few cents under it.
questions.simple: True, we put the stop a few cents under the day's low, then size the trade from that stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A flag is ours only above the ___-day simple moving average, the line below which we buy no longs.
questions.why: 200. We take no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long. The close holds above it on every flag session and at the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, every day of the flag. Below it there is no flag to buy.
questions.simple: The line is the 200-day. We buy no longs below it, and a flag only counts above it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: While a flag forms, what does volume usually do?
choices: It shrinks through the pause
It stays at pole volume
It grows as buyers pile in
It equals breakout volume
questions.answer: It shrinks through the pause
questions.why: It shrinks. Zanger: volume generally contracts during the pause, with an increase on the breakout. Bulkowski: the volume trend is down in 74% of flags that break up. That makes it the usual case, not a law.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet in the flag, loud on the break.

wrong.It stays at pole volume: Zanger: volume contracts during the pause. A rest as loud as the pole is not a quiet rest.
wrong.It grows as buyers pile in: Zanger: volume contracts in the pause, it does not grow. Rising volume belongs to the breakout.
wrong.It equals breakout volume: Zanger: volume contracts in the pause and increases on the breakout. The two stages differ.

questions.simple: Volume usually shrinks while a flag forms, then picks up on the breakout.

deeper.example: BB rested four days on 0.28x the pole's volume. PANW rested four days on half the pole's volume. Both were quiet rests, as the pattern usually shows.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-006, how strict the volume rule is)
+2 a statistic that changes (Bulkowski's 74%, updated 2020)

questions.q: The flag buy is a market order when the trigger level trades, in regular hours, from an alert set the night before.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We enter with a market order when the trigger level trades, in regular hours only. Set the alert at the level the night before. No new buys outside regular trading hours.
questions.lesson_line: Alert tonight, market order tomorrow, regular hours only.
questions.simple: True, we buy at market when the trigger level trades, in regular hours, from an alert set the night before.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.q: Which flag in a run is the one we want most?
choices: First after a breakout or correction
The third, once the trend is well proven
Any flag; the shape is all that counts
The one with the deepest pullback
questions.answer: First after a breakout or correction
questions.why: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction. That is the best one on our card. The second is normal. The third or later flag in one run without a proper base is graded B- or passed.
questions.lesson_line: First flag, best flag. Each one after it is later in the run.

wrong.The third, once the trend is well proven: Later flags sit later in the run. Our card marks down a third flag in one run that has no proper base.
wrong.The one with the deepest pullback: Our A+ depth is a third of the pole or less, and 10% or less from the top. Deepest is not best.
wrong.Any flag; the shape is all that counts: The shape is the same every time. Where it sits in the run is not.

questions.simple: The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is best, because later flags come late in the run.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed grade row, not a web source
+1 fixed before (a choice was shortened)

questions.q: Which stocks make the flags we trade?
choices: Leaders with high RS in strong groups
Laggards about to catch up
Any stock with the right shape
Whatever is loudest in the news
questions.answer: Leaders with high RS in strong groups
questions.why: Leaders, with an RS rating of 80 or more in one of the strongest groups. Bonde: flags are the most common continuation patterns on momentum leaders. A flag continues a run that was already strong.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the leader's flag. A laggard's flag is just a pause in a laggard.

wrong.Laggards about to catch up: A flag is a continuation pattern. It continues what the leader was already doing.
wrong.Any stock with the right shape: The shape alone does not pay. The leader, the catalyst and the market do.
wrong.Whatever is loudest in the news: Loud is not leading. We pick leaders by RS rating and by group strength.

questions.simple: We buy flags in leaders, meaning stocks with an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: A stop at the flag's low usually sits within about 3% of the buy.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The flag's low is the idea's invalidation, not the default stop, and it is almost never a 3% stop. It can sit 8% to 15% away, which means sizing too big or skipping the stop-width check.
questions.lesson_line: The flag low is where the idea dies. The day's low is where the trade does.
questions.simple: False. A stop at the flag low is almost never within 3% of the buy, so ours goes under the day's low.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62) and the card's proposed stop line (D-002)

questions.q: The flag's third day trades above the pole's high. What is it now?
choices: A breakout, no longer a flag
Still a flag; the rest goes on
A failed flag, so it is dead
A high tight flag, a stronger one
questions.answer: A breakout, no longer a flag
questions.why: A breakout. A flag that makes a higher high than the pole is no longer a flag. It has broken out of the pattern.
questions.lesson_line: The pole top is the lid. Above it the rest is over.

wrong.Still a flag; the rest goes on: A flag that makes a higher high than the pole is no longer a flag. The rest is over.
wrong.A failed flag, so it is dead: After the entry, a close under the flag's low means the idea is dead. Clearing the pole top is the opposite.
wrong.A high tight flag, a stronger one: The name depends on the pole's size, a near-double, not on clearing the top.

questions.simple: A flag that trades above its pole top has broken out. It is no longer a rest, so it is no longer a flag.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (the card's line, c05)

questions.q: Our card passes a stock whose 50-day is above the 200-day but flat over the last ten sessions.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Our card wants the 50-day above the 200-day and higher than it was ten sessions ago. A flat 50-day is not higher, so it fails. The card also wants the close above the 50-day. The 200-day line alone is not enough.
questions.lesson_line: A leader's lines point up and stack in order. Check them before the flag.
questions.simple: False, because our card wants the 50-day higher than it was ten sessions ago, and a flat line is not higher.

reasons: one cited fact only (c02)
a card proposal, not a rulebook rule (B26 is only the 200-day line)

questions.q: The day before the trigger is an inside day. What does that give you?
choices: A nearer stop for your buy
A warning the flag is dying
A reason to buy the inside day
A wider stop to ride out noise
questions.answer: A nearer stop for your buy
questions.why: A nearer stop. An inside day or a narrow-range day right before the trigger gives a nearer stop. Bonde: the day before the breakout should be a narrow-range or down day.
questions.lesson_line: A tight day before the trigger is a small stop waiting to be used.

wrong.A warning the flag is dying: A quiet, narrow day is what a healthy rest looks like. Heavy red days are the warning.
wrong.A reason to buy the inside day: The inside day is the tell, not the buy. The trigger level still has to trade.
wrong.A wider stop to ride out noise: It is the other way round. An inside day or a narrow-range day gives a nearer stop, not a wider one.

questions.simple: A tight day just before the trigger gives a nearer stop. Our card counts it as a cue for the best flags.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's tightness cue, with Bonde as the only web source

questions.q: One flag trade: full size at one price with one stop, no starter, no adds, no averaging down.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A flag trade is the full size at one price with one stop. No starter, no adding to the trade, no averaging down. Adding to a flag trade or averaging down is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, one size. No starter, no adds.
questions.simple: True, we buy the full size once, at one price, with one stop, and never add or average down.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)
+1 fixed before (the lesson line read as permission to add)

questions.q: On a flag trade, when does our first sell come?
choices: Into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or 3R
Only at 3R; never by the clock
Only at the measured move target
Never; let the whole trade run
questions.answer: Into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or 3R
questions.why: Both ways are ours. The first sell is not always counted in R. Often it is time-based: we sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, which can be 10, 12 or 20R. A third at 3R is one way we also teach. Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days.
questions.lesson_line: Sell the first piece into a strong push, by days or by R.

wrong.Only at 3R; never by the clock: Not only. Our first sell is often time-based, into a push of a few days, not just a set number of R.
wrong.Only at the measured move target: Our first sell is set by R or by the days of the push, not by a measured move.
wrong.Never; let the whole trade run: Our plan trims in stages and trails the last part. It does not let the whole trade run.

questions.simple: We sell the first piece into a strong push of a few days, or at a set multiple of our risk.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi, a respected breakout trader, sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days and then moves the stop to breakeven. We sell by days too, and by R. Both take some profit early and trail the rest.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: Closes ride the 10-day average and never tag the 21-day EMA. How does our card read that flag?
choices: Stronger; buyers never let it sag
Weaker; it never tested support
Equal; the two read the same way
Not a flag; it must tag the 21-day
questions.answer: Stronger; buyers never let it sag
questions.why: Stronger. Our card reads riding the 9 or 10-day average through the flag as the top version. Tagging the 20 or 21-day EMA and reclaiming it reads lower. Every close still has to hold the rising 21-day EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Riding the 10-day reads stronger than tagging the 21-day and reclaiming it.

wrong.Not a flag; it must tag the 21-day: Tagging the 21-day is allowed, not required. Every close just has to hold the rising 21-day EMA.
wrong.Weaker; it never tested support: Not testing the 21-day is not a flaw. Our card puts riding the 10-day above tagging the 21-day and reclaiming it.
wrong.Equal; the two read the same way: They differ. Our card reads riding the 9 or 10-day as the top version and tagging the 20 or 21-day and reclaiming it as a lower one.

questions.simple: Closes that ride the 10-day average read stronger than a flag that has to tag the 21-day and reclaim it.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed grade row
+1 fixed before (the old B- note leaned on a pending rule)

questions.q: By our card, does this rest pass the tightness test?
choices: Yes; the rest's bars are smaller
No; a 2.9% range is too shallow
No; four sessions is too short
Yes; a 36% pole makes any rest tight
questions.answer: Yes; the rest's bars are smaller
questions.why: Yes. The flag's average daily range is smaller than the pole's, 1.5% against 4.5%. Bulkowski: a tight flag performs better than a loose one; a loose one meanders and looks jagged.
questions.lesson_line: Tight means smaller bars than the run. Jagged means pass.

wrong.No; a 2.9% range is too shallow: Shallow is not a fault. PANW's four sessions in a 2.9% range was the tightest of our ten examples.
wrong.No; four sessions is too short: Four sessions is a normal rest. AMD, RARE, BB and PANW each rested four sessions.
wrong.Yes; a 36% pole makes any rest tight: Pole size is not the test. Tightness compares the flag's average daily range with the pole's.

questions.story: After a 36% pole the stock pauses four sessions in a 2.9% range. The flag's bars average 1.5% a day. The pole's bars averaged 4.5% a day.
questions.simple: Yes, because the rest's bars average 1.5% a day against the pole's 4.5%, and that is what tight means.

deeper.example: PANW, trigger 2020-12-03. A 36% pole, then four sessions only 2.9% deep on 0.53x the pole's volume. Buy 48.98, stop 48.29, a 1.4% stop. It reached 26.4R.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's range rule
+1 fixed before (a wrong count of four-day rests was corrected)

questions.q: On flag day four price dips under the 21-day EMA at noon, then closes back above it on light volume. What is that?
choices: Allowed; the flag is not broken
The flag is over; stand aside
A heavy red day; the grade drops
Allowed; the 21-day line is optional
questions.answer: Allowed; the flag is not broken
questions.why: Allowed. The card tests closes, not ticks: every flag close must sit at or above the rising 21-day EMA. An intraday undercut that closes back above is allowed. It is not a break. It is not a heavy red day either, which needs a red close on heavy volume.
questions.lesson_line: An undercut that closes back above the line is allowed. Only the close counts.

wrong.The flag is over; stand aside: The close is what counts, and it closed back above the line.
wrong.A heavy red day; the grade drops: A heavy red day is a red close on 1.5 times average volume or more. This one came on light volume.
wrong.Allowed; the 21-day line is optional: The line still matters. Every flag close must sit at or above it. Only the noon dip is forgiven.

questions.simple: Allowed, because only the close counts and this one closed back above the 21-day EMA.

reasons: one cited fact only (c10)
rests on a held decision (D-047, the one-close grace)
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: A flag entry more than 10% above the 10-day average is still fine if the pole was strong.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Too stretched to buy: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. A flag right after a parabolic burst waits until the 10-day catches up.
questions.lesson_line: Let the averages catch up. A stretched flag is a chase with a shape.

questions.q: Bought at 62.80 with the stop at 61.65. R is the fill minus the stop. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 66.25. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill. The hard rule is a third off at 3R. SHOP's pole top, 66.57, sits close by but plays no part.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: Three R is 66.25, because you add three times your risk per share to the 62.80 you paid.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (a third off at 3R, B19)

questions.q: A flag's pole was an earnings gap. It is five sessions old and the next report is months away. Does the earnings rule allow a buy?
choices: Yes; a post-earnings flag is fine
No; any flag after earnings is banned
Only if the pole's gap was under 4%
Yes, but only at half the usual size
questions.answer: Yes; a post-earnings flag is fine
questions.why: Yes. A post-earnings flag is fine. The blackout is only the 3 sessions before a report, and the next report is months away. Five of our ten examples had the report inside the pole.
questions.lesson_line: A flag after the report is fair game. The wait is before it.

wrong.No; any flag after earnings is banned: The ban is on buying in the 3 sessions before a report. After it is allowed.
wrong.Only if the pole's gap was under 4%: The 4% rule is about chasing past the trigger, not about the pole's gap.
wrong.Yes, but only at half the usual size: The earnings rule does not cut size. The grade sets the size, not an old report.

questions.simple: Yes, a flag after earnings is fine. We only avoid new buys in the 3 sessions before a report.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22) and the held earnings-flag decision (D-025)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A pause that makes higher highs and higher lows is a ___ up, not a flag.
questions.answer: wedge
questions.why: Wedge. A pause with higher highs and higher lows is a wedge up, not a flag. Zanger: a bull flag has lower tops and bottoms, and unlike a wedge its trend lines run parallel.
questions.lesson_line: Rising highs in the rest means it is wedging up. That is not the pattern.
questions.simple: The word is wedge. A flag leans against the run, so rising highs and lows make a wedge instead.

reasons: card rule with one agreeing web source

questions.q: A flag trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. The stop still applies the whole time, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days with nothing to show is an answer. Take the money elsewhere.
questions.simple: True, if a flag trade is still under 1R after 10 trading days, we sell it and free the money.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Buy here, and why?
choices: No; it is 4.8% past the level
Yes; it is only 2.40 above the level
Yes; but at half the usual size
No; any move above 50.00 is a chase
questions.answer: No; it is 4.8% past the level
questions.why: No. The level is 50.00 and the stock trades 52.40, which is 4.8% above it. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. Half size does not change the price.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent past the level, the trade is gone. The next trigger is not.

wrong.Yes; it is only 2.40 above the level: A move of 2.40 over a 50.00 level is 4.8%, past the 4% limit.
wrong.Yes; but at half the usual size: Half size does not fix a chase. The limit is the price, not the shares.
wrong.No; any move above 50.00 is a chase: A chase is more than 4% above the buy point. A fill a few cents over 50.00 is still inside the limit.

questions.story: Your trigger is the break of yesterday's high at 50.00. You were away from the screen and are not in. By 10:20 the stock is trading 52.40.
questions.simple: No, because 52.40 is 4.8% above the 50.00 trigger, which is past our 4% limit on chasing.

deeper.trap: The trap is the strong move itself. A stock running past your level feels like proof, so you pay up. But the rule is a price limit. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Here the level is 50.00 and the stock trades 52.40. Miss it and wait for the next trigger.

reasons: a computed key (4.8%)
rests on the owner's rulebook (the 4% no-chase limit, C28)

questions.q: The low before the run was 25.00. The pole top is 29.50. How big is the pole, in percent?
questions.why: 18%. Divide the pole top by the low before it and subtract one. Measure from the low, not the top. Kullamagi's own big move runs 30% to 100% or more, and Bulkowski wants a straight-line run. This question only measures the pole.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the pole first. The rest only matters if the run was real.
questions.simple: The pole is 18 percent, found by dividing the top by the low before it and taking away one.

reasons: a computed key
rests on a held decision (D-029, the pole size line), kept out of the key

questions.q: Pole low 30.00, pole top 45.00, flag low 39.00. What share of the pole did the flag give back, in percent?
questions.why: 40%. Take the drop from the pole top to the flag low and divide it by the pole's height, not by the price. Our card reads depth as a share of the pole, such as a third of it. Bonde notes that momentum movers often correct very shallowly.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the give-back against the pole, not against the price.
questions.simple: The flag gave back 40 percent, because the drop is divided by the height of the pole, not the price.

reasons: a computed key
rests on a held decision (D-046, how deep a flag may go), no verdict given
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: Fill 83.26. The day's low is 81.23 and the stop sits five cents under it. How far below the fill is the stop, as a percent of the fill?
questions.why: 2.5%. The stop is five cents under the 81.23 low, so it sits at 81.18. Divide the gap to the fill by the 83.26 fill, not by the stop. That is inside the 3% the stop usually sits within. It matches RARE's stop, 81.18.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The stop is 2.5 percent below the 83.26 fill, because the gap is divided by the fill, not the stop.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (the stop under the day's low, A3 and F62)

questions.q: What does that second close under the 21-day EMA do to the flag?
choices: It ends the flag; we stand aside
It changes nothing; the low holds
It is allowed; wait one more session
It only matters on heavy volume
questions.answer: It ends the flag; we stand aside
questions.why: It ends the flag. By our current default, a close under the rising 21-day EMA that is not reclaimed the next session ends the flag. Day six closed under it and day seven closed under it again. An intraday undercut that closes back above is allowed. This was a close.
questions.lesson_line: A close under the line that is not reclaimed the next session ends the flag.

wrong.It changes nothing; the low holds: Before the entry the test is a close under the rising 21-day EMA, not the flag low.
wrong.It is allowed; wait one more session: You waited one session already. Day seven closed under it again.
wrong.It only matters on heavy volume: The 21-day line is judged on the close, not the volume. Heavy red days are a separate warning.

questions.story: You have not bought yet. Day six of a flag closes under the rising 21-day EMA. Day seven closes under it again, on average volume.
questions.simple: It ends the flag. A close under the 21-day line that is not won back next session ends it, and day seven closed under again.

deeper.trap: An intraday undercut and a close under are different things. A dip under the 21-day EMA at noon that closes back above is allowed and is often the buy. Only the close counts, and here two closes sat under.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-047, a provisional default)
+2 a rule that may change when the owner rules
+1 fixed before (re-keyed on the adopted default)

questions.q: Buy the break today?
choices: No; a report inside 3 sessions
Yes; the flag is perfect
Yes; sell before the report
No; a 40% pole is extended
questions.answer: No; a report inside 3 sessions
questions.why: No. We take no new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report, and this report is two sessions away. A perfect flag now is one to watch, not buy.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings in two days is a gap you cannot stop. Wait for the other side of it.

wrong.Yes; the flag is perfect: A perfect shape does not lift the blackout. The report is two sessions away, inside the 3.
wrong.Yes; sell before the report: Buying inside the blackout and selling before the report still breaks the rule. No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report.
wrong.No; a 40% pole is extended: Stretch is measured against the 10-day average, not the pole's size. We skip a long more than 10% above it.

questions.story: A tight four-day flag after a 40% pole. Today it trades over the prior day's high. The company reports in two sessions.
questions.simple: No, because the report is two sessions away and we take no new buys in the 3 sessions before earnings.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Buy the break, or wait?
choices: Wait for a proper base to form
Buy; the trend is already proven
Buy now, with a tighter stop
Wait for a fourth flag to confirm
questions.answer: Wait for a proper base to form
questions.why: Wait for the base. The third or later flag in one run without a proper base is graded B- or passed. Our card says to wait for the base.
questions.lesson_line: Three flags and no base is a run that needs a rest, not another buy.

wrong.Buy; the trend is already proven: A proven trend is a late one here. Our card grades the third flag B- or passes it.
wrong.Buy now, with a tighter stop: The stop sits where the honest stop is. A tighter one does not fix a third flag with no base.
wrong.Wait for a fourth flag to confirm: A fourth flag in the same run is later still. Our card says to wait for the base.

questions.story: The stock is on its third daily flag in four weeks. No base has formed between them. Today it ticks over yesterday's high.
questions.simple: Wait for a base. A third flag in a short run with no base is late, so our card says to wait for the base.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed grade row
+1 fixed before (an unsupported quote was removed)

questions.q: Once the flag trade fills, the stop can wait in your head until the first red day.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. The stop is the exit and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A real stop with the broker. Your head is not a broker.
questions.simple: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, because a stop in your head is not a stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, A4)

questions.q: Bulkowski draws a line on how long a flag can run. Where is it?
choices: Under 3 weeks, else a rectangle
Up to 12 weeks, then a rectangle
Under 1 week, else a rectangle
At least 7 to 8 weeks, like a base
questions.answer: Under 3 weeks, else a rectangle
questions.why: Under 3 weeks. Bulkowski: flags are short, less than 3 weeks long, and longer patterns are rectangles or channels. ChartSchool ideally sees one to four weeks and calls a flag over 12 weeks old a rectangle. IBD says most sound bases take at least seven to eight weeks. A rest that long is a base, not a flag.
questions.lesson_line: A flag is a short rest, under 3 weeks by Bulkowski. Longer is a rectangle, or a base.

wrong.Up to 12 weeks, then a rectangle: That is ChartSchool's outer line. Bulkowski draws it under 3 weeks, and ChartSchool ideally sees one to four weeks.
wrong.Under 1 week, else a rectangle: Too short. Bulkowski: flags are short, less than 3 weeks long; longer patterns are rectangles or channels.
wrong.At least 7 to 8 weeks, like a base: That is IBD's floor for a sound base. A flag is far shorter.

questions.simple: Bulkowski says a flag lasts less than 3 weeks. Anything longer is a rectangle or a channel.

deeper.counter: The sources disagree at the edge. Bulkowski cuts a flag off under 3 weeks. ChartSchool ideally sees one to four weeks and calls a flag a rectangle only past 12 weeks. Learn the line as Bulkowski's, and treat a longer rest as a base.

reasons: +2 sources disagree at the edge, so the numbers are a convention
+2 rests on a held decision (D-045, how long a flag may rest)
+1 fixed before (three quotes were added to the cited facts)

questions.q: Grade each.
choices: First flag A+; third flag B- or pass
Both A+; the shape is identical
Third flag A+; the trend is proven
questions.answer: First flag A+; third flag B- or pass
questions.why: The first flag A+, the third B- or a pass. The first flag after a base breakout or a market correction is the A+ row; the third or later flag is the B- row.
questions.lesson_line: Same shape, different grade. Count the flags before you count the shares.

wrong.Both A+; the shape is identical: The shape is one row of the grade. Which flag it is sits in another row.
wrong.Third flag A+; the trend is proven: Proven means late. The third flag in one run is the B- row or a pass.

questions.story: Two stocks, the same tight four-day flag. One is the first flag after a base breakout. The other is the third flag in a long run with no base.

questions.q: Which break do Bonde, Zanger and ChartSchool trust more?
choices: The 2.1x day closing at the high
The 0.7x day; quiet is better
Equal; the level is all that matters
Neither; a break needs a catalyst
questions.answer: The 2.1x day closing at the high
questions.why: The 2.1x day closing at the high. Bonde: breakout-day volume should be higher and the stock should close near its high. Zanger: volume increases on the breakout. ChartSchool: an expansion of volume on the break lends credence. The trigger is still the level trading.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume and a strong close make a break more trusted. Quiet and mid-range make it less.

wrong.The 0.7x day; quiet is better: Quiet belongs inside the flag. The break wants buyers showing up.
wrong.Equal; the level is all that matters: The level is the trigger. The day's volume and close are what the sources check.
wrong.Neither; a break needs a catalyst: A catalyst helps make the pole. It does not decide between these two breaks.

questions.story: Two identical flags. One breaks out on 0.7x its average volume and closes mid-range. The other breaks on 2.1x and closes at the high.
questions.simple: The day on 2.1 times normal volume that closes at its high is the stronger break.

deeper.trap: A strong close on light volume is not enough. QCOM's trigger day closed at the high on 0.76x volume, was the top, and the next session took the stop. UIS cleared the flag's high on 2.3x volume and ran for six weeks.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-006, the breakout volume line)

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take fewer shares than planned
Tighten the stop; full size
Buy full size; risk more
Buy a starter, the rest later
questions.answer: Take fewer shares than planned
questions.why: Take fewer shares. Stop first, and the size comes from the stop. Here the honest stop sits 4.6% away. That is inside the 5% we accept, but wider than the 1% to 3% we prefer, so it buys fewer shares. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.

wrong.Tighten the stop; full size: The honest stop is where the idea fails. Stop first; the size comes from the stop.
wrong.Buy full size; risk more: Shares = account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop. A wider stop means fewer shares, not more risk.
wrong.Buy a starter, the rest later: No starter, no adding. The full size at one price with one stop.

questions.story: You plan to buy the break at 48.60. The honest stop, a few cents under the day's low, sits 4.6% away. You wanted full size.
questions.simple: Take fewer shares. Set the stop first and let it set the size, and never move the stop closer to buy more.

deeper.counter: A wide honest stop is a reason for fewer shares, not a reason to hide the stop. Chasing works the same way: the stop stays put, the distance grows, and the shares shrink.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3) and a held cap decision (D-005)
+1 fixed before (a long sentence was split)

questions.q: Buy the break?
choices: No; let the 10-day catch up
Yes; the flag is a textbook one
Yes; a 12% stretch is quite normal
No; five days is too short a flag
questions.answer: No; let the 10-day catch up
questions.why: No. We skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. This one sits 12% above, so let the average catch up first.
questions.lesson_line: Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. Let the average catch up first.

wrong.Yes; the flag is a textbook one: A tidy shape does not lift the stretch rule. Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.
wrong.Yes; a 12% stretch is quite normal: Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. Twelve is past it.
wrong.No; five days is too short a flag: Five days is a normal rest. The trouble is the stretch above the 10-day, not the length.

questions.story: A one-day gap made the whole pole. Five days later a tidy flag sits 12% above the 10-day average and ticks over yesterday's high.
questions.simple: No, because the stock sits 12% above its 10-day average, which is too stretched to buy.

deeper.trap: A tidy flag is not enough. The test is the stretch: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
+1 fixed before (the lesson line claimed a one-gap pole is never a leader's run, which the card does not say)

questions.q: A tight flag in a stock that trades $6 million a day. Our rule?
choices: Skip; under $20 million a day
Buy; the shape is what counts
Buy small; a thin stock needs less
Buy; only the $10 price floor counts
questions.answer: Skip; under $20 million a day
questions.why: Skip. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day, and this one trades $6 million. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Thin names are not watched, let alone flagged.

wrong.Buy; the shape is what counts: The shape does not fill your exit. Dollar volume does.
wrong.Buy small; a thin stock needs less: It is not on the list at all. Illiquid stocks are not even watched, so no size makes it a buy.
wrong.Buy; only the $10 price floor counts: The $10 floor is on the share price. Daily dollar volume has its own floor of $20 million.

questions.simple: Skip it. We only trade stocks that trade at least $20 million a day, and this one trades $6 million.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, D42)

questions.q: Account 60,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 20.09, stop 19.81. How many shares?
questions.why: 1071. Risk is 0.5% of 60,000. Divide that by the fill minus the stop, 20.09 minus 19.81, and round down. The size is the smaller of this and the position cap, 40% of the account. 1071 shares fit under it. AMD's 1.4% stop set the size, not the other way round.
questions.lesson_line: Risk dollars over the stop distance, rounded down, then check the cap.
questions.simple: The size is the risk dollars divided by the gap between 20.09 and 19.81, rounded down to 1071 shares.

deeper.trap: The trap is skipping the cap check. Risk alone can give a size that is too big for the account. The size is the smaller of the risk size and the position cap. Here the cap does not bind, but you check it every time.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5 sizing, A7 cap)
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: If a flag trade opens above 3R, the first trim waits until the stock trades back down to 3R.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. If a stock opens above a trim level, 3R or 5R, take that trim at the open. The level has already come. Waiting for it to trade again is not the rule.
questions.lesson_line: A trim level the open jumps past is a trim at the open.
questions.simple: False, because a stock that opens above a trim level gets that trim taken at the open.

reasons: one cited fact only (h25)
rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.q: What do those two days do to the flag?
choices: They end it; it is distribution
They drop it a grade, no more
Nothing; only break volume counts
They raise it; weak holders sold out
questions.answer: They end it; it is distribution
questions.why: They end it. A red close on 1.5 times the 50-day average volume or more is a heavy red day, and 1.8 is over that line. One such day drops the grade. Two end the flag as distribution, not a rest.
questions.lesson_line: One heavy red day is a mark against. Two is supply, and the rest is over.

wrong.Nothing; only break volume counts: Volume is read inside the flag too. Zanger: it should contract during the pause.
wrong.They drop it a grade, no more: One such day drops the grade. A second ends the flag.
wrong.They raise it; weak holders sold out: Heavy red volume is selling. Two or more such days are distribution, not a rest.

questions.story: Days three and five of a flag each close red on 1.8 times the 50-day average volume. Every other day was quiet.
questions.simple: Two heavy red days end the flag. It is distribution, not a rest.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed volume thresholds
+1 fixed before (a choice was shortened)

questions.q: What does that close mean?
choices: Idea dead; your stop hit first
Widen the stop to the flag low
Hold; the pole still counts for it
Buy more; it is a cheap re-entry
questions.answer: Idea dead; your stop hit first
questions.why: The idea is dead. After the entry, a close under the flag's low means the idea failed. The stop at 30.95 sits above that close, so normally it was hit first and you were out. The flag low at 29.80 is the invalidation line, not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: By the time price closes under the flag low you should be long gone.

wrong.Widen the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up. The flag low was never the stop; it is the line that says the idea failed.
wrong.Hold; the pole still counts for it: The pole was the past. A close under the flag low says the run is over for now.
wrong.Buy more; it is a cheap re-entry: You are already out. A new buy needs a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop.

questions.story: You bought at 31.40 with the stop at 30.95. Two weeks later the stock closes at 29.40, under the flag's low of 29.80.
questions.simple: The idea is dead, and your 30.95 stop would normally have sold you before this close.

deeper.example: The planned loss was the gap from the 31.40 fill down to the 30.95 stop. The flag low at 29.80 sits lower, so a close under it normally tells you nothing new: you were out already.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's invalidation line and the owner's stop rule
+1 fixed before (a choice was shortened and a false citation removed)

questions.q: What changes?
choices: Smaller size and fewer positions
Only the grade changes, not the size
No flags at all until it turns Green
Full size; they are first flags
questions.answer: Smaller size and fewer positions
questions.why: Smaller and fewer. The market reading is a guide: Green is full risk per grade, and Yellow is smaller and fewer. The flags are the same, so you trade fewer of them with less risk.
questions.lesson_line: Yellow means the same flags with less money behind them.

wrong.No flags at all until it turns Green: Red is mostly cash. Yellow still trades, smaller and fewer.
wrong.Full size; they are first flags: Full risk per grade belongs to Green. In Yellow the reading says smaller and fewer, even for first flags.
wrong.Only the grade changes, not the size: Size changes too. Yellow means smaller and fewer, even for clean first flags.

questions.story: The reading turns Yellow. Your list has three clean first flags at their triggers.
questions.simple: A Yellow market means smaller size and fewer trades, even for clean first flags.

reasons: rests on the owner's market reading (F65)

questions.q: The last third of a fast-moving flag trade. What takes it out?
choices: A close under the 10-day
A dip under the flag low
A close under the 50-day
Any red day, even a small one
questions.answer: A close under the 10-day
questions.why: A close under the 10-day. Our default trail is the 10-day for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. We sell on a close below it. It rides the last third, after a third at 3R and a third at 5R. Kullamagi also trails the rest with the 10- or 20-day.
questions.lesson_line: The last third rides the line. The close below it is the exit, not a dip under it.

wrong.A dip under the flag low: Price normally hits the stop well before the flag low. The last third is sold on a close under the trail average.
wrong.A close under the 50-day: The 50-day is not our trail. The default trail is the 10-day or the 21-day, sold on a close below it.
wrong.Any red day, even a small one: One red day is not the rule. The close below the trail average is.

questions.simple: The last third is sold when a day closes under the 10-day average, since this is a fast mover.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook trail default (E52), which is adjustable

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job: a small planned loss
Proved the entry was a mistake
Wrong; it should wait for a close
Too tight; a wider stop is the fix
questions.answer: Its job: a small planned loss
questions.why: Its job. The stop is the exit. STZ reached 0.85R, hit the stop on day 2, then ran to 50 without us. Our card counts seven in ten fixed-stop entries coming back to the stop before 3R. The small stop and the next trigger are the answer.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working. The next trigger is the answer, not a wider stop.

wrong.Wrong; it should wait for a close: The stop is a real order with the broker, not a close you wait for. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Proved the entry was a mistake: Our card counts seven in ten fixed-stop entries coming back to the stop before 3R. A stop-out is the cost of the plan, not proof of a mistake.
wrong.Too tight; a wider stop is the fix: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, and it only moves up, never down or wider. A stop-out is the cost of the plan.

questions.story: A four-day flag 3.1% deep on a quarter of the pole's volume. You buy the break at 44.34, stop 43.55. It reaches 0.85R, then day two's low of 43.07 takes you out. The stock later runs to 50.
questions.simple: The stop did its job. A small planned loss is the plan working, even when the stock runs on later.

deeper.trap: The later run to 50 tempts you to call the stop wrong. That is hindsight. A stop is judged by the plan, not by what came after. The same small stop on the next trigger is still the rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)
the seven-in-ten count is our own scan

questions.q: Bought at 48.98, stop 48.29. R is the fill minus the stop. The stock trades to 52.43. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. The move from 48.98 to 52.43 is five times the risk per share. This is where the second third comes off, after the first at 3R. PANW went on to 26.4R at its best.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is the second trim.
questions.simple: That is 5R, because the gain from 48.98 to 52.43 is five times the risk per share.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (a third at 5R, E51)

questions.q: What is the stop now?
choices: First 30-minute low; out past 2R
Still 61.65; sell at the open
No stop at all; wait for close
Buy more at open to lower cost
questions.answer: First 30-minute low; out past 2R
questions.why: The first 30-minute low of the gap-down day is the new stop. The first 30 minutes decide, so you do not sell blind at the open. The ceiling: if they take the loss past 2R, get out. This is the one exception to a stop that only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets 30 minutes, not a new opinion.

wrong.Still 61.65; sell at the open: The stop was gapped over. The gap rule is the one exception: the first 30-minute low is the new stop.
wrong.No stop at all; wait for close: The close is hours away. The first 30 minutes decide, and past 2R you are out.
wrong.Buy more at open to lower cost: No adds and no averaging down. The full size goes in at one price with one stop, and a gap loss is not a reason to buy more.

questions.story: Your flag long filled at 62.80 with the stop at 61.65. Next morning it opens at 61.10 on sector news.
questions.simple: After a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop, and past 2R you are out.

deeper.trap: The pull is to sell at once or to hope. The rule does neither. It waits for the first 30-minute bar and uses its low as the stop. If that low puts the loss past 2R, you are out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook gap rule (B20)
fixed before: the open was moved so the 2R ceiling does not apply

questions.q: By our card's pole test, bull flag or high tight flag?
choices: A high tight flag
An ordinary bull flag
A long flat base
A simple pullback
questions.answer: A high tight flag
questions.why: A high tight flag. Measure the pole first: a high tight flag follows a near-double, and a bull flag follows a smaller run. A run of 110% is more than a double. A 15-session rest is also too short for a flat base, which rests at least 25. Bonde names both flags as the momentum leader's patterns.
questions.lesson_line: The pole names the setup. A near-double is the other lesson.

wrong.An ordinary bull flag: A 110% run in six weeks is more than a double. That pole belongs to the high tight flag.
wrong.A long flat base: Fifteen sessions is too short for a flat base, which rests at least 25.
wrong.A simple pullback: A pullback has no pole. This stock ran 110% first, so there is a pole to name.

questions.story: The stock ran 110% in six weeks on a product launch. Now it pauses 15 sessions a little under the high.
questions.simple: The pole decides it. A run of 110% is more than a double, so this is a high tight flag.

deeper.trap: A big run is not enough on its own. Measure the pole, then count the rest. Here the run is 110% in six weeks and the rest is 15 sessions. A near-double with a short rest is the high tight flag. A smaller run is the bull flag.

reasons: a number rule that is still pending (D-048, D-049)
rests on a held decision
fixed before: the numbers were moved so the key holds under every option

questions.q: Bull flag or flat base?
choices: A flat base setup
A bull flag
A wedge up
A VCP setup
questions.answer: A flat base setup
questions.why: A flat base setup. Count the sessions: a flag is a short rest. Bulkowski says flags run under 3 weeks, and longer patterns are rectangles or channels. Our flat base rests at least 25 sessions in a box up to 15% deep, with a flat ceiling tapped twice.
questions.lesson_line: A rest measured in weeks is a base. Count the sessions before you name it.

wrong.A bull flag: Nine weeks is far past a flag. Bulkowski: flags run under 3 weeks, and longer patterns are rectangles or channels.
wrong.A wedge up: A wedge up makes higher highs. This box has a flat top tapped twice.
wrong.A VCP setup: A VCP strings two to six pullbacks, each smaller than the last. This box has one flat ceiling, tapped twice.

questions.story: After a 35% run the stock has rested nine weeks in a box 9% deep. The flat top has been tapped twice.
questions.simple: A rest nine weeks long in a flat box is a flat base, not a flag, because flags are short.

deeper.counter: Sources differ on where a flag ends. ChartSchool calls a flag a rectangle only past 12 weeks, so its line would still allow nine weeks. Bulkowski says under 3 weeks, and our card says 15 sessions. Nine weeks is a base on our count.

reasons: the flag length is still pending (D-045)
rests on a held decision
the flat ceiling tell is the card's alone

questions.q: Which pattern is this?
choices: A VCP setup
A bull flag
A high tight flag
A flat base
questions.answer: A VCP setup
questions.why: A VCP, a volatility contraction pattern. Look for shrinking pullbacks. A flag is one short drift on lighter volume. A VCP strings several pullbacks, each smaller than the last, before its pivot. Here three pullbacks over 30 sessions each shrink.
questions.lesson_line: One drift is a flag. A string of shrinking swings is the VCP lesson.

wrong.A bull flag: Three pullbacks over 30 sessions is not one short drift. That is the volatility contraction pattern.
wrong.A high tight flag: The story gives no doubling pole, and the rest is too long and too structured for a flag.
wrong.A flat base: A flat base is a long, flat box with a tapped ceiling. These pullbacks shrink each time, which is the VCP tell.

questions.story: Over 30 sessions the stock makes three pullbacks, each shallower than the last, volume drying on each. The last one is a few percent deep.
questions.simple: Three pullbacks that each get smaller make a VCP. A flag is only one short drift.

deeper.trap: The lookalike to rule out is the flat base, which is a long, flat box with a tapped ceiling. A VCP is different: each pullback is smaller than the one before it, and the pivot sits at the end. Count the pullbacks before you name it.

reasons: the VCP tell rests on the card's line alone
fixed before: choices rebalanced

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A moving-average pullback
A bull flag on a steep run
A flat base resting for weeks
A high tight flag on the 20-day
questions.answer: A moving-average pullback
questions.why: A moving-average pullback. Find the pole: a pullback to the 10, 20 or 50-day with no pole is its own setup, not a flag. Bulkowski says no straight-line run, no flag. An 8% grind over six weeks is not a straight-line run.
questions.lesson_line: No run, no flag. A drift to the 20-day after a grind is a pullback lesson.

wrong.A bull flag on a steep run: An 8% grind over six weeks is not a steep run. No pole, no flag.
wrong.A high tight flag on the 20-day: A high tight flag follows a near-double. An 8% grind over six weeks is nowhere near one.
wrong.A flat base resting for weeks: A flat base rests at least 25 sessions in a box with a flat ceiling tapped twice. This one climbed, then dipped three days to a line.

questions.story: A leader climbs in a slow, steady channel, up 8% over six weeks, then drifts three days down to its 20-day EMA on light volume.
questions.simple: With no steep run before it, the dip to the 20-day is a pullback, not a flag.

deeper.trap: The pole is what makes a flag a flag. A stock that grinds up slowly and then dips to its moving average has no run to rest from. Judge it as a moving-average pullback, which has its own rules.

reasons: the pole size is still pending (D-029), but the key holds under every option
fixed before: a flagged question

questions.q: What is it now?
choices: A base, no longer a flag
A bull flag, A grade
A flag that failed
A flag, but only graded B-
questions.answer: A base, no longer a flag
questions.why: A base. Our card calls a rest past 20 sessions a base, and this pause is 21 sessions old. Bulkowski says flags run under 3 weeks. It held 6.6% deep on 0.81x the pole's volume, so nothing failed. It simply stopped being a flag.
questions.lesson_line: A flag that keeps resting becomes a base. Past 20 sessions, stop calling it a flag.

wrong.A bull flag, A grade: Twenty-one sessions is past the card's 20-session line and past Bulkowski's 3 weeks.
wrong.A flag that failed: Nothing failed. It held 6.6% deep on 0.81x the pole's volume. It just stopped being a flag and became a base.
wrong.A flag, but only graded B-: Our B- band stops at 20 sessions. At 21 it is a base, not a flag.

questions.story: A 30% pole, then a pause only 6.6% deep on 0.81x the pole's volume. The pause is now 21 sessions old.
questions.simple: A pause of 21 sessions is too long for a flag, so it is now a base.

deeper.trap: A pause that has run past the flag length is judged as a base, not a flag. It can still be a good setup, only under different rules. Count the sessions from the pole top, and do not let a clean, quiet look keep the word flag alive.

reasons: rests on the card's 20-session line (c06)
21 sessions is a base under D-045 options A and B; option C (up to 2 months) would make it a flag

questions.q: A flag that closed under its 21-day EMA on two straight sessions can still be bought on the next prior-day-high break.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Two closes under the 21-day EMA end the flag. The buy needs a flag that is still on; the next one is a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the line twice and the flag is gone. Wait for the next setup, not the next tick.

questions.q: What did the stop do?
choices: Its job; the leader simply failed
Cost you; it needed more room
Nothing; you should have added lower
questions.answer: Its job; the leader simply failed
questions.why: Its job. The trigger day closed at the low of its range, the next session's low took the stop, and the loss was 1.78%. A planned loss is the system working.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out for 1.78%. That is the cost of being there for the ones that run.

wrong.Cost you; it needed more room: More room is a bigger loss on the same failed break. The stop only moves up.
wrong.Nothing; you should have added lower: No adding, no averaging down. A failed break is an exit, not a sale.

questions.story: You buy the prior-day-high break at 276.33, stop 271.41. The day closes at the low of its range, 271.99. Next morning the low of 270.60 takes you out.

questions.q: Bought at 66.62, stop 64.78. You sell a third at 72.14. How many R did that third bank?
questions.why: 3R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. TSEM took nine sessions to get there and then ran past 100.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The first third is 3R.

questions.q: By our rules, what was sold on the way to 6R?
choices: A third at 3R, a third at 5R
Nothing; hold it all to the trail
All of it, sold at 3R
Only a third, taken at 3R
questions.answer: A third at 3R, a third at 5R
questions.why: Two thirds came off: a third at 3R and a third at 5R. The hard rule is a third at 3R, and the trade reached 6R, so both levels were hit. The 5R level is adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. The trims are the part the market cannot take back.
