wrong.All of it, sold at 3R: The first trim is a third. The next third comes at 5R, then the trail takes the rest.
wrong.Only a third, taken at 3R: It reached 6R, past the 5R level, so the second third came off too.
wrong.Nothing; hold it all to the trail: The hard rule is a third at 3R, then another third at 5R. Only the last third rides the trail.

questions.story: A four-day flag after a near-vertical pole. You bought at 80.41, stop 78.66. It reached 6R in two weeks, then rolled over.
questions.simple: A third is sold at 3R and another third at 5R, and the trade went to 6R, so both came off.

deeper.example: Take the story's trade. A third came off at 3R and a third at 5R before the move rolled over. Only the last third was left to give back its gain. The two trims were already banked.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook trims (B19, E51)
the 5R level is adjustable

questions.q: Hold through the report? Pick the rule that decides it.
choices: No; hold through only if up 5R
Yes; the setup was graded A+
Yes; move the stop to breakeven first
No; hold through only if up 3R
questions.answer: No; hold through only if up 5R
questions.why: No. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R, and this one is up 2R. A gap on the news can jump any stop, so a breakeven stop or a good grade is no cushion. Three R is the first trim, not the holding line.
questions.lesson_line: Five R buys the ticket through earnings. Two R does not.

wrong.Yes; move the stop to breakeven first: A gap can jump a breakeven stop. The rule asks for 5R, and this trade is up 2R.
wrong.Yes; the setup was graded A+: The rule asks for 5R, not a grade. This trade is up 2R.
wrong.No; hold through only if up 3R: Three R is where the first third comes off. The holding line is 5R.

questions.story: Your flag long is up 2R and the company reports tomorrow after the close.
questions.simple: No, because a trade is held through a report only when it is up 5R, and this one is up 2R.

deeper.trap: A breakeven stop feels like free protection, but an overnight gap can open below it. The gap rule then makes the first 30-minute low the new stop. A loss past 2R in that time means you are out.

reasons: the key rests on one fact (h08)
rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Brooks's 'bull flag' means any pullback in a bull trend, so it is the same setup as ours.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Brooks calls a bull flag a minor reversal down in a bull trend. It can be one sideways bar or most of the last leg up. Ours needs a pole. Same name, different idea.
questions.lesson_line: Same words, different pattern. Ours starts with a pole.
questions.simple: False. Brooks uses the same name for any small pullback, but our flag needs a steep run first.

deeper.trap: The same words can name two ideas. Brooks counts a one-bar pause as a bull flag. A search for the name in his material will list pauses that our card would not call a flag.

reasons: one publisher for the Brooks side
the card's pole line is the other half

questions.q: By our card, take it or pass?
choices: Pass; the lines are not stacked up
Take it; price is above the 200-day
Take it; the pole is strong
Pass; the flag is only five days
questions.answer: Pass; the lines are not stacked up
questions.why: Pass. Our card wants the 50-day above the 200-day and rising, with the close above the 50-day. Here the 50-day is still under the 200-day. Our rulebook only bars longs below the 200-day, so this extra test is the card's own.
questions.lesson_line: Check the lines before the flag. Stacked and rising, or pass.

wrong.Take it; price is above the 200-day: Price above the 200 is one line. By our card the 50 under the 200 fails the other.
wrong.Take it; the pole is strong: The pole is the pattern. The averages are the context, and they are out of order.
wrong.Pass; the flag is only five days: Five days is a normal short rest for a flag. The fault is in the averages, not the length.

questions.story: A 40% pole and a tidy five-day flag. Price is above the 200-day, but the 50-day still sits under the 200-day after a long decline.
questions.simple: The 50-day average is still under the 200-day, so by our card the stock has not fully recovered and we pass.

deeper.counter: The rulebook line is looser than the card. Price above the 200-day passes the rulebook's long test. The card adds that the 50-day must be above the 200-day and rising. A stock repairing a long decline can pass the first test and fail the second.

reasons: the stacked-and-rising test is the card's proposal, not a rulebook rule
rests on the owner's 200-day line (B26)

questions.q: What is the lesson of this stop-out?
choices: A weaker setup than a first flag
A stop set too close to entry
A pole too small to trust
A flag too deep to be bought
questions.answer: A weaker setup than a first flag
questions.why: A weaker setup than a first flag. The first flag after a breakout or correction is the best one, and this one came late in a long run. The stop was not the problem: it sat 2.25% under the entry, a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: The stop pays for the lesson. Here the lesson was how late the flag came, not its shape.

wrong.A stop set too close to entry: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low by rule. A wider stop is not the fix; the setup was the weak spot.
wrong.A pole too small to trust: A 30% pole is a normal bull flag pole. The weak spot was how late the flag came.
wrong.A flag too deep to be bought: The flag was only 3.8% deep after a 30% pole. Depth was not the problem.

questions.story: A five-day flag, 3.8% deep, at all-time highs after a 30% pole, late in a long run. You buy at 957.53, stop 935.95. It makes 0.56R and is stopped on day three.
questions.simple: A flag late in a long run is weaker than a first flag. The stop only took the planned loss.

deeper.trap: How late a flag comes is a judgment, not a measured edge. The stop sat 2.25% under the entry. A late flag in an extended stock was weaker before the entry. The stop did what it was there to do.

reasons: the flag-count grade is the card's proposal
the count is UCT's own read, not a measurement

questions.q: A flag in a stock with 2 million shares a day. Your stop and risk allow 60,000 shares. Our rule?
choices: No more than 20,000 shares
No more than 10,000 shares
No more than 40,000 shares
No more than 60,000 shares
questions.answer: No more than 20,000 shares
questions.why: No more than 20,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 2 million is 20,000. The stop sets one limit, here 60,000 shares. The volume rule sets another. The size is the smaller. Splitting the buy into pieces does not change what you own.
questions.lesson_line: Size is the smaller of what the stop allows and what the stock's volume can carry.

wrong.No more than 10,000 shares: That is under the cap. The rule is 1% of average daily volume, and 1% is more than this.
wrong.No more than 40,000 shares: That is twice the volume cap. We never own more than 1% of average daily volume.
wrong.No more than 60,000 shares: The stop sets one limit. One percent of the day's volume sets another, and it is smaller here.

questions.simple: We can own at most 1% of the average daily volume, which is 20,000 of the 2 million shares.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a split buy slips under the cap. Three pieces still leave you owning 60,000. The cap is on what you own, not on any one order, so it counts the whole position. Work out the volume cap first, then check the stop size against it.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42 volume cap, A5 sizing)

questions.q: What kind of buy was that?
choices: An early entry on the same setup
A separate setup of its own
A buy that breaks the rules
A confirmed breakout entry
questions.answer: An early entry on the same setup
questions.why: An early entry on the same setup. By our current default the flag-top break defines the flag. The prior day's high is an earlier trigger level on the same flag, with the same stop rule. BB bought at 80.41, before its 82.12 high broke.
questions.lesson_line: The flag-top break defines the flag. An earlier trigger is the same setup with the same stop rule.

wrong.A separate setup of its own: By our current default it is the same flag with an earlier trigger, not a new setup.
wrong.A buy that breaks the rules: A market order when a trigger level trades is the rule. The prior day's high is a trigger level.
wrong.A confirmed breakout entry: The flag's high of 82.12 has not broken, so nothing is confirmed yet. This buy comes before the break, which is why it is early.

questions.story: Four quiet days on a quarter of the pole's volume. You buy the prior-day-high break at 80.41, stop 78.66. The flag's high of 82.12 is still above you.
questions.simple: Buying the prior day's high is an earlier trigger on the same flag, with the same stop rule.

deeper.trap: Do not treat the early buy as a looser rule. Its stop is still a few cents under the day's low, and the same grade cues apply. Only the trigger level moved earlier: 80.41 here, under the flag's high of 82.12.

reasons: which trigger defines the flag is still pending (D-027)
keyed on a provisional default
fixed before: re-keyed by the resolver

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
choices: Market over 66.26; day-low stop; 3R
Limit under 66.26; mental stop; 3R
Market over 66.26; mental stop; no trim
Buy the close; day-low stop; no trim
questions.answer: Market over 66.26; day-low stop; 3R
questions.why: Buy at market as it trades through 66.26, with a stop a few cents under the entry day's low. Take a third off at 3R. Write it before the open, with entry, stop and size down on paper. Every position also gets a real stop order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim, trail. Write it before the open.

wrong.Limit under 66.26; mental stop; 3R: A limit under the level never fills on the break. A stop kept in your head is not a stop.
wrong.Market over 66.26; mental stop; no trim: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, and the plan includes a third off at 3R.
wrong.Buy the close; day-low stop; no trim: The trigger is the trade through the level, not the close, and the plan includes a third off at 3R.

questions.story: Eight quiet days after a doubled pole, every close holding the 21-day EMA. Tonight you plan tomorrow's buy at your trigger level, 66.26.
questions.simple: Buy at market when the level trades, with a stop a few cents under the day's low. Sell a third at 3R.

deeper.example: The plan written tonight: set the alert at 66.26. Tomorrow, buy at market if it trades through. Put a real stop a few cents under that day's low. Sell a third at 3R and another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, E57, D39, D41)
fixed before: the stop wording was clarified

questions.q: What now?
choices: Sell a big part into strength
Add; the trend is accelerating
Hold it all for the measured move
Nothing; let the trail handle it
questions.answer: Sell a big part into strength
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long, a burst of gaps and expanding bars, is sold into. It is a judgment call. Kullamagi says leaders move in stair steps: a move, a sideways rest, then another move.
questions.lesson_line: When the whole move happens in three days, that is the strength to sell into.

wrong.Add; the trend is accelerating: We never add to a flag trade. The full size goes in at one price with one stop.
wrong.Hold it all for the measured move: Our rule is to sell a big part into a climax run, not to hold it all for a target.
wrong.Nothing; let the trail handle it: The trail is for the part you keep. Our rule is to sell a big part into a climax run, and the burst is the time to do it.

questions.story: Three weeks after your flag buy the stock gaps up three mornings in a row on rising volume. It closes far above its 10-day.
questions.simple: A burst of gaps like this is a climax, so sell a big part into the strength.

deeper.trap: The trap is to read three gap-ups as proof the trend will go on. A climax is a burst of gaps and expanding bars far above the 10-day. The rule is to sell a big part into it, and it is a judgment call, not a number.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34), which is a judgment call
fixed before: story split

questions.q: After a flag stop-out, you buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. After a stop-out we buy again only if the setup triggers again. It is a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Liking the stock is not a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out means flat. The next trade needs its own trigger.
questions.simple: True. Being stopped out leaves you flat, and a new buy needs a new trigger, not just a good feeling.

deeper.trap: Wanting back in is the pull. A stop-out leaves you flat, and liking the stock is not a trigger. The rule asks one question: has the setup triggered again? If yes, it is a new trade with a new stop, sized fresh. If no, you stay flat.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21)

questions.q: What does the strong close tell you about this flag's odds?
choices: No promise; strong closes failed too
A promise; it almost never fails
Move the stop to breakeven
Sell it; the volume was too low
questions.answer: No promise; strong closes failed too
questions.why: No promise on its own. Three of our four failures closed the trigger day at the high and still failed. Bonde wants a close near the high on a higher-volume breakout day, but here volume was low. That is a mark against it, not an exit. The leader, the market and the stop decide the trade.
questions.lesson_line: A good close is a good grade, not a promise. The stop stays where it is.

wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not on a good first close.
wrong.Sell it; the volume was too low: Low volume is a mark against the buy, not an exit. The stop is the exit.
wrong.A promise; it almost never fails: QCOM, STZ and LLY all closed the trigger day at the high and were stopped within days.

questions.story: Your flag buy closes its first day at the high on below-average volume.
questions.simple: A strong close is not a promise. Three of our four failures closed the trigger day at the high and still failed.

deeper.example: Two of the failures show it. QCOM closed the trigger day at the high on 0.76x volume and was the top. STZ closed at the high on 0.32x volume and was stopped on day 2. A strong close graded the day, but the stop decided the trade.

reasons: the breakout volume line is still pending (D-006)
the count of failures is our own scan

questions.q: What is the better plan?
choices: Wait for the tight day; stop under it
Buy today; use the flag low as the stop
Buy today at half the usual size
Buy today with a 3% stop instead
questions.answer: Wait for the tight day; stop under it
questions.why: Wait for the tight day. An inside day or narrow-range day right before the trigger is the A+ tightness cue, because it gives a nearer stop. Bonde wants the day before a breakout to be a narrow-range or down day. The stop comes first and the size comes from it. A 4.6% stop today can fit inside 3% tomorrow if the day stays tight.
questions.lesson_line: A tighter day is a tighter stop. One more day of patience buys the size.

wrong.Buy today; use the flag low as the stop: The flag low is the invalidation, not the stop. It is almost never a 3% stop.
wrong.Buy today at half the usual size: Fewer shares is allowed, but the stop is still 4.6% wide. The tight day can bring it inside 3%.
wrong.Buy today with a 3% stop instead: The stop is a few cents under the day's low, set first. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. Do not squeeze the stop.

questions.story: The flag's wide day four leaves the honest stop 4.6% under the break. The stock looks ready to print a narrow inside day tomorrow.
questions.simple: A narrow day right before the trigger gives you a nearer stop, so waiting a day is the better plan.

deeper.trap: Size follows the stop, never the reverse. Cutting shares to fit a wide stop is allowed, but it does not make the stop nearer. Forcing the stop to 3% when the honest stop is 4.6% puts the stop where the setup does not.

reasons: rests on the owner's stop-first rule (A3) and the 3% habit (A13)
fixed before: the half-size note

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a prior-day-high break. Read the flag against its rising 21-day EMA. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it; every close held the line
Pass; two closes sat under it
Pass; the pole was too small
Take it; the rest ran four days
questions.answer: Take it; every close held the line
questions.why: Take it. An eight-day flag held the 21-day EMA on every close, after a doubled pole. An intraday undercut that closes back above is allowed.
questions.lesson_line: The flag that never closes under its fast line is the one worth the alert.

wrong.Pass; two closes sat under it: Look again: every close of the flag sits on or above the 21-day EMA.
wrong.Pass; the pole was too small: The pole nearly doubled in 12 days. Small is not the word.
wrong.Take it; the rest ran four days: The rest ran eight sessions, not four. Count the bars on the chart before you give a reason.

questions.simple: Every close of this flag held the rising 21-day line, so the flag is intact and we take it.

deeper.example: The pole was 99% in 12 days to 66.57. The flag then ran eight sessions between 59.50 and 66.26 on 0.85x the pole's volume. Every close held the rising 21-day EMA.

reasons: a chart question read off our own bars
the 41.7R run is from our own scan

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades over the prior day's high. Look at the slope of the highs through the pause. Take it or pass?
choices: Pass; the highs rose; a wedge up
Take it; the pole was 58%
Take it; it is only 10.7% deep
Pass; the flag ran too long
questions.answer: Pass; the highs rose; a wedge up
questions.why: Pass. The highs rose 5.6% across the 7-day pause. Higher highs and higher lows through the rest is a wedge up, not a flag. Zanger: a bull flag has lower tops and lower bottoms, slanting against the trend, with parallel lines.
questions.lesson_line: A rest that climbs is not resting. Flat or down is the flag; up is the pass.

wrong.Take it; the pole was 58%: The pole was fine. The pause after it climbed, and a climbing pause is a wedge up.
wrong.Take it; it is only 10.7% deep: Depth is not the fault here. The slope of the highs is.
wrong.Pass; the flag ran too long: Seven sessions is a normal short rest. The fault is the climbing highs, not the length.

questions.simple: The highs climbed across the pause, which makes it a wedge up and not a flag, so we pass.

deeper.counter: Depth and pole alone would pass this one. The pause was only 10.7% deep after a 58% pole, so it looks like a neat flag. The slope of the highs is what fails it: they rose 5.6%.

reasons: the wedge-up line is the card's proposal
a chart question read off our own bars

questions.q: Which stock has the A+ pole on our card?
questions.story: Two stocks pause after a run. Stock A jumped 45% in five sessions on an earnings gap. Stock B drifted up 35% over fifteen sessions on no news.
choices: Stock A, fast with a catalyst
Stock B, a steady climb
Both poles grade the same
Neither; a pole must double first
questions.answer: Stock A, fast with a catalyst
questions.why: Stock A. On our card, the A+ pole is 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst such as an earnings gap. Stock B rose 35% over fifteen sessions on no news.
questions.lesson_line: The A+ pole is big, fast and has a reason.

wrong.Both poles grade the same: They do not. Our card's A+ pole is the one made fast on a catalyst.
wrong.Neither; a pole must double first: Doubling is the pole of the high tight flag. The A+ pole for a bull flag is 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst.
wrong.Stock B, a steady climb: Stock B had no catalyst. Our card's A+ pole is 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst.

questions.simple: Stock A has the A+ pole because it rose over 30% fast on an earnings gap. Stock B had no catalyst.

reasons: rests on the card's grade row for the A+ pole

questions.q: Before the pole, the lowest low was 40.00. What price is 30% above it?
questions.why: 52.00. Add 30% to the low of 40.00. On our card, a pole of 30% or more, made fast on a catalyst, is the A+ pole.
questions.lesson_line: Know the 30% line before you call a pole A+.
questions.simple: Add 30% to the low to find the price where the pole reaches the A+ line.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the card's grade row

questions.q: Which flag has the A+ depth on our card?
questions.story: Two flags follow strong poles. Flag A gave back 20% of its pole and sits 12% under the top. Flag B gave back 30% and sits 9% under the top.
choices: Flag B; it passes both of the tests
Flag A; it gave back less of its pole
Both; each passes one of the tests
Neither; both gave back too much
questions.answer: Flag B; it passes both of the tests
questions.why: Flag B. Our card's A+ depth cue needs both: a third of the pole or less, and 10% or less from the top. Flag B gave back 30% and sits 9% under the top, so it clears both. Flag A gave back 20%, which is fine, but sits 12% under the top, so it fails one.
questions.lesson_line: Our card's A+ depth: a third of the pole or less, within 10% of the top.

wrong.Flag A; it gave back less of its pole: Flag A passes the pole test but sits 12% under the top. The card needs both.
wrong.Both; each passes one of the tests: Flag B passes both tests. Flag A fails the 10% test.
wrong.Neither; both gave back too much: Flag B gave back 30%, under a third of the pole, and sits 9% under the top. It passes both.

questions.simple: Flag B has the A+ depth, because it passes both the one-third and the 10% tests.

deeper.example: Flag B gave back 30%, under a third of the pole, and sits 9% under the top, inside 10%. Both hold. Flag A gave back 20%, under a third, but sits 12% under the top, over 10%. Only one holds. The card asks for both, so Flag A is not the A+ depth.

reasons: one cited fact only (c45)
the card's depth cue is a proposal, not a settled rule
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: The pole top is 60.00 and the flag low is 56.00. How far under the top is the low, as a percent of the top?
questions.why: 6.7%. Take the top minus the low, 60.00 minus 56.00, and divide by the top, not by the low. On our card, 10% or less from the top is one part of the A+ depth cue, and 6.7% fits it. The other part is a third of the pole or less.
questions.lesson_line: Measure depth from the top, in percent.
questions.simple: The low is 6.7 percent under the top, found by dividing the drop by the 60.00 top.

reasons: one cited fact only (c45)
the card's depth cue is a proposal, not a settled rule
a computed key
fixed before by the checker

questions.q: You would buy at 56.60. The 10-day average is 50.00. How far above the 10-day is the buy, in percent?
questions.why: 13.2%. Take the buy price minus the 10-day average and divide by the average, 50.00, not by the buy price. That is past 10%. Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Check the stretch before you buy. Over 10% above the 10-day, skip.
questions.simple: The buy is 13.2 percent above the 10-day, because the gap is divided by the 50.00 average.

reasons: one cited fact only (h13)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
a computed key

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Skip a long that is more than ___% above its 10-day average.
questions.why: 10. Too stretched to buy: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. The 4% in the no-chase rule is a different limit, measured from the buy point, not from the 10-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Over 10% above the 10-day is too stretched. Wait for the averages.
questions.simple: The blank is 10, because we skip a long that is more than 10 percent above its 10-day average.

reasons: one cited fact only (h13)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)

questions.q: Where does the stop go now?
questions.story: You bought a flag break at 20.09 with the stop at 19.81. The stock reaches 3R and you sell the first third.
choices: Up to your entry price
Down to give it more room
Cancel it; a third is banked
Switch to the 10-day trail now
questions.answer: Up to your entry price
questions.why: Up to your entry, 20.09. Our card moves the stop to breakeven at the first trim; the rulebook says between 2R and 5R. The stop only moves up, never down or wider, and it stays a real stop order with the broker.

questions.q: Is the flag still a buy?
questions.story: A tight flag rests on the 21-day EMA. On two of its days the stock closed red on 1.6 times its 50-day average volume. Today is quiet.
choices: No; that is distribution, not a rest
Yes; the flag held the 21-day EMA
Yes; heavy red days are normal in flags
No; any red close ends a flag
questions.answer: No; that is distribution, not a rest
questions.why: No. Two or more heavy red days in the flag is distribution, not a rest. Each closed red on 1.6 times its 50-day average volume, past the 1.5 line. Holding the 21-day EMA does not rescue it.
questions.lesson_line: Two heavy red days is selling, not resting.

wrong.Yes; the flag held the 21-day EMA: Holding the 21-day EMA is a separate test. Two heavy red days end the flag anyway.
wrong.Yes; heavy red days are normal in flags: Heavy red days are selling, not resting. Two or more of them in the flag is distribution.
wrong.No; any red close ends a flag: Only a heavy red day counts: red on 1.5 times average volume or more. A plain red close does not end a flag.

questions.simple: Two heavy red days mean heavy selling, so this is distribution, not a rest, and the flag ends.

deeper.trap: Holding the 21-day EMA is a separate test. A flag can sit on the line and still be sold into. Count the heavy red days: one drops the grade, two end the flag. A quiet day today does not erase them.

questions.q: The 50-day average volume is 1,800,000 shares. A red flag day trades 2,700,000. How many times average is that?
questions.why: 1.5 times. Divide the day's volume of 2,700,000 by the average of 1,800,000. That is right on the line: on our card, a red day on 1.5 times average volume or more is heavy.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the day's volume by the average. 1.5 times or more is heavy.
questions.simple: Divide the day's volume by the average to get 1.5 times, which is right at the heavy line.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a flag break two days ago. The stock is down about half an R and your stop has not traded. A post on your feed says the market looks weak.
choices: Hold the position as planned
Sell half now to be safe
Widen the stop for room
Move the stop up to entry
questions.answer: Hold the position as planned
questions.why: Hold. After the entry, the stop is the exit, with the time stop. Your stop has not traded, and a post on your feed is not an exit. The stop only moves up. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days.
questions.lesson_line: After the entry, the stop is the exit. Not a post, not a hunch.

wrong.Sell half now to be safe: A post is not an exit. The stop is, along with the time stop after 10 trading days under 1R.
wrong.Widen the stop for room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Move the stop up to entry: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, at the first trim. The stock is below your entry now, so that stop would hit at once.

questions.simple: The stop is the exit, so you hold until it trades or the time stop sells the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, C33)
